newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-CHRISTMAS PRESENT UEFA COULD HAVE DONE WITHOUT.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CHRISTMAS PRESENT UEFA COULD HAVE DONE WITHOUT.

text.p: UEFA officials returning from their holidays on Monday will not be happy with the seasonal gift awaiting them from the French judiciary -- allegations that the Tapie affair is as far-reaching as many people suspected.
Bernard Tapie, ex-president of former European champions Marseille, is expected to go on trial in May in France in a case that could blow the top off European soccer.

According to an investigative report on Marseille, details of which were reported in the daily Le Monde on Thursday, the former European champions misspent some $19 million on rigging matches and transfers under Tapie's presidency.
Twenty people, including middlemen on the run from the law as well as the respected former France coach Michel Hidalgo, are implicated in some 50 cases of match fixing.
It is hardly the scenario France want little more than a year before they host the 1996 World Cup finals.
But the French are not the only country with the stench of match-fixing in the air.

Portugal is currently wrestling with such allegations while in England this month the trial opens of three former top flight players, including Zimbabwe's former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar, accused of match fixing.
The 205-page French report dated December 13, which has not been published, was drawn up so a court could determine whether the findings justify a trial.

"The most illegal tricks were used in player transfers to make sure that the best would join (Olympique Marseille)," the paper said, citing the report on the club's accounts by magistrate Pierre Philipon.

Tapie, who allegedly pumped funds into reducing to a minimum the risks involved in football matches between 1987 and 1993, was found out when the Valenciennes bribery case broke weeks after Marseille won the European Cup in 1993.

He is awaiting the result of an appeal against a two-year jail sentence for his part in the case in which three players of lowly Valenciennes were bribed to ensure Marseille did not lose a French league match near the end of the 1992-93 season.

Tapie is alleged to have fixed at least three major European Cup ties in the early 1990s when Marseille -- French champions five years in succession although later stripped of the fifth title -- were regular competitors and reached the final twice.

One of the matches in question, against Bruges of Belgium in 1993, paved the way for Marseille to reach the final in which they won 1-0 against the AC Milan of his big Italian rival Silvio Berlusconi.

Several middlemen, including the Greek Spiros Karageorgis who is the subject of an international arrest warrant, are alleged to have made illegal payments to players from a number of different countries.

UEFA have not been available to comment. But their reactions to allegations of bribery of referees in the past have varied, although they were quick to suspended Dynamo Kiev early last season after they attempted to bribe the Spanish referee of one of their European Cup games.
